title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke: What CROATOAN Really Meant

scenes.label: OUTER BANKS, AUGUST 1590
lines: August 1590. Off the coast of what is now North Carolina, an English ship lies at anchor near a dark island.
The sailors row toward the shore. They sound a trumpet, and sing familiar English songs into the trees.
Nobody answers.
Their leader, Governor John White, has been away for three years. On this island, he left more than a hundred colonists, including his own daughter and his baby granddaughter.
The next morning, on a post at the gate of the settlement, he finds a single word carved into the wood.
Croatoan.
Four centuries later, we are still trying to read it.

scenes.title: England's first attempts
lines: In March 1584, Queen Elizabeth granted Walter Raleigh a charter to plant an English colony in America.
The first settlement, in 1585, was a military outpost of about a hundred men under Ralph Lane.
It went badly. In June 1586, the men sailed home with Sir Francis Drake's fleet.
Raleigh tried again. This time, not with soldiers, but with families.
In 1587, about one hundred and fifteen men, women and children crossed the Atlantic under their governor, the artist John White.
They were meant to settle on Chesapeake Bay. But the pilot, Simon Fernandes, refused to take them any farther than Roanoke Island.
They arrived on July 22nd, 1587. Soon after, a colonist named George Howe was ambushed and killed.

scenes.label: 18 AUGUST 1587
lines: Then, on August 18th, White's daughter Eleanor gave birth to a girl.
She was named Virginia Dare. The first English child born in the Americas.
Supplies were short. The colonists asked White to sail back to England for help.
On August 27th, he left. Before he went, he wrote that they were preparing to move about fifty miles into the mainland.

scenes.title: Three years away
lines: White reached England late in 1587. Then history got in the way.
In 1588, the Spanish Armada threatened England, and every good ship was needed at home.
White did set out that spring with two small ships. They were attacked and looted at sea, and both turned back.
It took him until 1590 to get a passage, aboard privateering ships.

scenes.label: 17 AUGUST 1590
lines: When they finally reached the Outer Banks, the sea was rough.
One boat overturned in the surf. Of the eleven men in it, seven drowned.
White's crew went on anyway. That night came the trumpet, and the songs, and the silence.
They landed on August 18th, 1590. Virginia Dare's third birthday.
On a tree, they found three carved letters. C, R, O.
Then, on a post at the entrance to the settlement, in capital letters, the full word. Croatoan.

scenes.title: What White found
facts: A strong palisade around the site
Chests dug up and broken open
lines: The houses had been taken down, and the site was enclosed by a high wooden palisade.
Chests had been buried and dug up again. White's own books were torn, his maps rotten, his armour rusted through.
There were no signs of a struggle, and no sign that anyone had left in a hurry.
But here is the twist. Before he left, White and the colonists had agreed on a code.
If they moved, they would carve the name of the place they went. If they were in danger, they would carve a cross above it.
There was no cross.

scenes.title: Croatoan
facts: An island to the south, today part of Hatteras
Birthplace of Manteo, the colony's ally
lines: Croatoan was an island to the south, home to a Native people friendly to the English.
It was the birthplace of Manteo, a Croatoan man who had been to England and back, and who had helped the colony.
White wrote that he greatly joyed to find a certain token of their safe being at Croatoan.
To him, it was not a mystery. It was a forwarding address.

scenes.label: AUGUST 1590
lines: So why didn't he go and get them?
As the crew hauled up the anchor, the cable broke. They had one anchor left out of four.
The weather grew fouler and fouler. Food was short, and fresh water had been lost.
The captain decided to head south to resupply, then come back. But storms drove them toward England instead.
John White never saw America again.

scenes.title: The clues that followed
facts: Talk of men in European clothes
lines: When Jamestown was founded in 1607, the English searched again, and found nothing.
John Smith heard stories from Native leaders about men in European clothes living inland.
The writer William Strachey later claimed the colonists had been massacred. Historians still dispute it.
And around 1701, the explorer John Lawson visited Hatteras. The islanders told him some of their ancestors were white, and some of them had grey eyes.

scenes.title: Modern evidence
facts: 2012: a fort hidden under a patch on White's map
lines: Science has added new pieces.
Tree rings show 1587 had the worst growing season in eight hundred years. The colony arrived in a drought.
In 2012, researchers found that a patch on one of John White's own maps, in the British Museum, hides the symbol of a fort, about fifty miles inland.
Digs near that spot, called Site X, found sixteenth-century English pottery. Critics say it could come from later settlers.
On Hatteras, the old Croatoan, archaeologists have found part of a rapier and metal from clothing. Whether colonists lived there is still debated.
And beware of easy answers. In the 1930s, dozens of carved stones appeared, supposedly messages from Eleanor Dare.
Most were exposed as a hoax in 1941.
So were they really lost?
Maybe the colony split. Some went inland, some to Croatoan, and over the years they became part of the Native communities that sheltered them.
The word on the post was their message, and White understood it. He just couldn't get there.
Where do you think the colonists went? Tell me in the comments.

youtube.description:
In 1590, Governor John White returned to Roanoke Island after three years away and found his colony gone, with one word carved on a post: CROATOAN. We follow the 1587 colony, Virginia Dare's birth, the Armada delays, the secret code White agreed with the colonists, and the modern evidence from a hidden fort on White's own map to digs on Hatteras Island.

Scenes marked RECONSTRUCTION are illustrated dramatizations based on historical accounts. All illustrations are original artwork.
